title: One server-assembled run context for Do, Plan and scheduled runs: instruction stack, thread history, persona, memory and run notes
summary: Extract the ADR-0003 resolver (platform, org, Space, persona, summoned agent) that Ask turns already use into one shared function, add the missing fields to RunAgentRequest, and seed every Do, Plan and scheduled run with the resolved instructions, prior thread turns under the compaction budget, memory prefetch and attachments, with completeness flags on the run record. Automations later get a per-schedule notes block.
whyItMatters: Three consolidators found the same defect from different angles (runtime, extensibility, memory): the governed agent loop starts from a preamble plus the goal, so org policy, Space instructions, persona and memory are silently ignored exactly where the agent can take actions. Every reference agent inherits its conversation and instructions. It is the cheapest high-impact fix in the audit and it is a governance gap, not only a quality gap.

title: Durable agent loop: checkpoint every round and pause, resume in place after approval, answer or crash, close dangling tool calls, effect ledger
summary: Persist the Do loop's fold inputs in session-core at every round and before each effectful call, and add a continuation worker that re-enters the loop at the checkpoint when an approval, a clarifying answer or a crash recovery arrives, instead of re-executing three whitelisted effects from a cold descriptor. Close tool calls that never returned with typed closers, record effects in an exactly-once ledger, park turns whose providers are exhausted, and replay open interaction requests on reconnect.
whyItMatters: Today the LLM loop does not resume reasoning after an approval: only execute_provider_action, book_shipment and tickets.create are re-run from a descriptor. That makes every approval a dead end for multi-step tasks and blocks plan-continue, ask_user, scheduled runs with approvals, goals and the computer-use loop. Five of twelve references have durable resume; DeepSeek and Hermes show the exact mechanism.

title: Declared tool side-effect classes, a never-auto set and per-tool allow/ask/never policy, so MCP tools become callable through the signed gate
summary: Replace the substring classifier is_risky_tool with a declared SideEffectClass (read, read_sensitive, local_mutation, open_world_mutation, external_effect) bound in capability-core's trusted map for every built-in, provider action and discovered MCP tool (unknown defaults to external_effect), add a non-delegable never-auto set, and expose per-connector and per-tool allow/ask/never policy. With registry-owned capability bindings, MCP tools stop being refused by the gate and become usable in Do and, read-only, in Ask.
whyItMatters: The model cannot call any MCP tool today (plain chat strips mcp__ names; Do mode offers them but trusted_capability_id returns None so the gate refuses). MCP is table-stakes (6 of 12) and per-tool policy is the standard way references keep it safe. The substring classifier is also the weakest link in an otherwise strong signed-gate design: risk should be declared data, not guessed from names.

title: Approvals v2: scoped decisions, typed cause codes, decision provenance, denial memory and step-up for high-risk effects
summary: Extend the approval decision from approve/reject to once, this run, this thread or always-as-a-reviewed-rule (an 'always' on a card is held at session scope until confirmed in settings), remember denials within a run, and compute a typed ApprovalCause at the point each permission, hook, capability or browser-risk decision is made. whyItMatters: Approvals are already durable and stronger than most references (encrypted exact-effect descriptors, postcondition re-checks), but the cards say only that a tool requires approval and every decision is single-use, which produces approval fatigue and teaches users to click through. Codex, Claude and Antigravity show scoped decisions and typed causes as the fix.

title: Govern and prove the skill-learning loop: learned skills start as owner-scoped proposals, a seeded eval proves the loop, and a learning ledger supports undo
summary: Make every skill written by the background review a proposal owned by the user whose run produced it and not matchable by anyone else, with a Settings > Learning inbox (diff, reason, source run); promotion to org scope needs an admin decision. Then prove the loop end to end with a seeded eval (a real Do run authors a skill a later turn uses) and cost controls, and project memory and skill lineage into a 'What Verevon learned' ledger with undo and rollback.
whyItMatters: The learning loop runs by default and its candidates become org-wide matchable skills with no review, owner or scope. That is a data-governance risk (one user's run can change every colleague's agent) as well as a quality risk, and the loop has never been shown to produce a useful skill. Hermes, the reference for self-improvement, stages writes fail-closed and keeps a reversible ledger; Manus emits proposals.
